differential: Cervical radiculopathy
Bilateral arm paresthesias in a young adult can result from nerve root compression at the cervical spine level.
Thoracic outlet syndrome
Compression of the neurovascular bundle between the neck and shoulder can cause bilateral upper extremity paresthesias.
Carpal tunnel syndrome (bilateral)
Median nerve compression at both wrists can cause paresthesias, though typically more distal in distribution.
Vitamin B12 deficiency
Nutritional deficiency can cause symmetric peripheral neuropathy with paresthesias in the extremities.
Multiple sclerosis
Demyelinating disease can present with bilateral paresthesias in young adults as an initial manifestation.
eliminated: None
Insufficient information at this stage to definitively rule out any diagnoses.

differential: Radial nerve compression/Saturday night palsy
Bilateral wrist extensor weakness with paresthesias along posterior forearms and dorsal hand sensory loss are classic for radial nerve involvement.
Posterior interosseous nerve syndrome
Pure motor weakness of wrist extensors can occur with this radial nerve branch compression, though bilateral presentation would be unusual.
Lead poisoning (lead neuropathy)
Can cause bilateral radial nerve predominant motor neuropathy with wrist drop, particularly in young individuals with environmental exposure.
Cervical radiculopathy (C6-C7)
Bilateral cervical nerve root compression could produce posterior forearm paresthesias and wrist extensor weakness in this distribution.
Multifocal motor neuropathy
Can present with asymmetric weakness in young adults affecting specific nerve distributions, though sensory involvement makes this less likely.
eliminated: Carpal tunnel syndrome
Would affect median nerve distribution with palmar/first three digits involvement, not posterior forearm and dorsal hand.

differential: Radial nerve compression (Saturday night palsy)
EMG/NCS confirm bilateral radial nerve dysfunction at the elbow level with acute denervation, classic for compression neuropathy at the spiral groove.
Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies (HNPP)
Young age and bilateral nerve involvement at common compression sites suggests underlying genetic predisposition to pressure-induced neuropathies.
Lead poisoning
Can cause bilateral radial nerve palsy with predilection for wrist extensors, though typically associated with systemic symptoms.
Multifocal motor neuropathy
Can present with asymmetric weakness in young adults affecting specific nerve distributions, though usually more progressive.
Bilateral radial nerve entrapment syndrome
Repetitive activities or anatomical variants causing chronic bilateral compression at the spiral groove or radial tunnel.
eliminated: Cervical radiculopathy
EMG/NCS localize the lesion specifically to the radial nerve at the elbow, not the nerve root level.
Stroke/central lesion
Normal vital signs, bilateral peripheral nerve pattern on EMG/NCS, and sensory involvement indicate peripheral not central pathology.
Guillain-Barré syndrome
Focal radial nerve distribution rather than ascending symmetrical pattern, and no mention of areflexia or albumino-cytologic dissociation.

differential: Tourniquet-related radial nerve palsy
Prolonged tourniquet use (90 minutes) on the left upper extremity during recent surgery directly correlates with acute denervation and conduction deficits in the radial nerve distribution.
Perioperative positioning injury (bilateral radial nerve compression)
Bilateral radial nerve involvement with asymmetric severity suggests compression against hard surfaces during prolonged surgical positioning under anesthesia.
Saturday night palsy (radial nerve compression at spiral groove)
Although bilateral involvement is unusual, the clinical presentation matches radial nerve compression, though the surgical timing makes tourniquet injury more likely.
Compartment syndrome of the forearm
Post-surgical swelling following ACL repair with tourniquet use could cause compartment syndrome affecting the radial nerve, though the timing (one week post-op) makes this less likely.
Iatrogenic nerve injury from regional anesthesia
If regional anesthesia was used for the ACL surgery, direct needle trauma or hematoma formation could cause radial nerve injury, though tourniquet injury better explains the findings.
eliminated: Cervical radiculopathy
EMG/NCS localize the lesion to the radial nerve at the elbow rather than nerve root level, and there is no mention of neck symptoms.
Lead neuropathy
No exposure history mentioned and the acute onset immediately following surgery points to mechanical injury.
Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies (HNPP)
While this could predispose to compression injuries, the direct temporal relationship with prolonged tourniquet use makes acquired injury primary.

differential: Cervical radiculopathy
Bilateral arm paresthesias in a young adult can result from nerve root compression at the cervical spine level.
Thoracic outlet syndrome
Compression of the neurovascular bundle between the neck and axilla commonly causes bilateral upper extremity paresthesias in young patients.
Carpal tunnel syndrome (bilateral)
Median nerve compression at both wrists can cause paresthesias, though typically starts distally rather than generalized arm symptoms.
Vitamin B12 deficiency
Nutritional deficiency can cause symmetric peripheral neuropathy with paresthesias affecting multiple extremities.
Anxiety/hyperventilation syndrome
Psychogenic paresthesias are common in adolescents and young adults, often presenting bilaterally in the extremities.
eliminated: None
Insufficient information at this stage to definitively rule out any diagnoses.

differential: Cervical myelopathy
Hyperreflexia, bilateral upgoing Babinski signs, and upper extremity radicular symptoms suggest spinal cord compression in the cervical region.
Multiple sclerosis
Young age, bilateral upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, Babinski), and asymmetric sensorimotor deficits suggest demyelinating disease.
Syringomyelia
Central cord pathology can cause dissociated sensory loss, weakness, and hyperreflexia in upper extremities with pyramidal signs.
Subacute combined degeneration
Bilateral pyramidal tract involvement with paresthesias could indicate dorsal and lateral column pathology from B12 deficiency.
Posterior radial nerve palsy bilateral
Wrist extension weakness and dorsal hand sensory loss match radial nerve distribution, though hyperreflexia and Babinski signs suggest additional CNS pathology.
eliminated: Peripheral neuropathy
Hyperreflexia and upgoing Babinski signs indicate upper motor neuron involvement, incompatible with pure peripheral neuropathy which causes hyporeflexia.

differential: Radial nerve palsy with concurrent cervical myelopathy
EMG/NCS confirm bilateral radial neuropathy (worse on left), but hyperreflexia and upgoing Babinski signs indicate coexistent upper motor neuron pathology.
Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies (HNLPP)
Young patient with bilateral radial nerve compression at typical sites (elbow) and reduced conduction velocities suggests genetic predisposition to pressure-induced neuropathies.
Lead toxicity
Bilateral radial nerve involvement (wrist drop pattern) with upper motor neuron signs can occur in lead poisoning, affecting young adults.
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)
Combination of lower motor neuron findings (denervation, weakness) with upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, Babinski) fits motor neuron disease pattern, though unusual at age 18.
Bilateral radial nerve compression with unrelated spinal cord lesion
EMG/NCS confirm peripheral radial neuropathy from compression (Saturday night palsy), while separate pathology causes myelopathic signs.
eliminated: Pure radial nerve entrapment
Hyperreflexia and bilateral upgoing Babinski signs cannot be explained by isolated peripheral nerve lesion alone.
Guillain-Barré syndrome
Reflexes would be diminished or absent rather than hyperreflexic (3+).

differential: Tourniquet-induced radial nerve palsy
Prolonged tourniquet application (90 minutes) on the left upper extremity during recent ACL surgery directly correlates with the radial nerve dysfunction pattern and timeline.
Bilateral radial nerve compression neuropathy
EMG/NCS findings of reduced conduction velocity at the elbow bilaterally with acute denervation suggest compression at the spiral groove, though asymmetric severity favors tourniquet injury on left.
Cervical myelopathy with superimposed peripheral nerve injury
Hyperreflexia, upgoing Babinski signs, and bilateral upper extremity symptoms suggest cervical cord pathology with concurrent radial nerve injury from tourniquet.
Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies (HNLPP)
Bilateral radial nerve involvement with focal compression susceptibility after minor trauma (tourniquet) fits this genetic disorder predisposing to pressure palsies.
Perioperative positioning injury with cervical cord compression
Combined upper motor neuron signs and radial nerve findings could reflect poor surgical positioning causing both spinal cord and peripheral nerve injury.
eliminated: Isolated Saturday night palsy
The bilateral involvement, upper motor neuron signs, and clear tourniquet history make simple radial nerve compression from external pressure unlikely.
Posterior interosseous syndrome
This would not explain the sensory deficits on dorsum of hand or the upper motor neuron signs.

counterfactuals.alteration_description: The presence of hyperreflexia and upgoing Babinski sign argues against radial nerve injury, which would not cause upper motor neuron signs.
